newsitem.title: USA: "Elephant Man" may have had unrecognized disease.
newsitem.headline: "Elephant Man" may have had unrecognized disease.

text.p: Joseph Merrick, the disfigured "elephant man" whose story was told on stage and in film, did not suffer from the disease often named after him but from a different, very rare condition, it was reported on Tuesday.

Amita Sharma, a radiologist at The Royal London Hospital where Merrick's skeletal remains have been kept since his death in 1890, said in a report to the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America that the likely cause of his condition was Proteus Syndrome, a rare non-inherited condition. She said she based her conclusion on radiograph and computed tomographic studies of the skeleton.
It had been widely assumed Merrick suffered from neurofibromatosis -- sometimes called "elephant man disease" -- a genetic disorder of the nervous system that causes abnormal tissue growth.

The extremely rare Proteus Syndrome is a malfunction in cell growth that causes hypergrowth of bone and tissues in the body. Fewer than 100 cases of the incurable disease have been reported worldwide and it was first identified only about two decades ago, Sharma said.
Neurofibromatosis, which occurs in one out of every 4,000 live births, causes numerous soft, fibrous growths from nerves on the skin.

Merrick was born in 1862 and began an abnormal growth pattern at the age of 21 months. His head had a circumference of 36 inches (91 cm), compared to about 24 inches (61 cm) for most men. His body was covered with large, fleshy growths that made him a societal outcast.
He was befriended by a surgeon at the London hospital where he lived out his years. A Broadway play based on his life won a Tony Award in 1979 and was made into a movie the following year.

"His was obviously the most extreme form of the disease," which sometimes causes gigantism in just a victim's hand or foot, Sharma told Reuters. "It has a lot of different manifestations, that's why it's named after the Greek god Proteus, who could change his form to escape capture.
"If by imaging techniques we can diagnose this accurately, I think it will help people," she said.
